source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
finding: Controlled test of one agent versus four multi-agent topologies. Gains depend on whether the task splits into parts. Architecture-task fit decides the result, not agent count.
numbers: 260 configurations, 6 agentic benchmarks, 5 architectures, 3 LLM families. Best multi-agent change vs single agent ranges from +80.8% (decomposable finance reasoning, centralized) to -70.0% (sequential planning, independent).
limits: Google study; model fit is modest (cross-validated R2 0.373). Prompts, tools and token budget held equal, so results may shift with tuned prompts.
agent_relevance: Do not split a sequential reasoning task across several model calls. Keep one program-controlled thread.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems (capability saturation)
finding: Once a single agent already scores above about 45%, adding coordination gives negative returns.
numbers: Coefficient beta=-0.236, p=0.004 for single-agent baseline; the 45% threshold matches 94% of cells (binomial p<0.001).
limits: Threshold is empirical for these six benchmarks and these model tiers; may move as models improve.
agent_relevance: Spend coordination budget only where the single-pass baseline is weak.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems (error amplification)
finding: Architectures with no central check amplify errors. A central verifier contains them.
numbers: Trace-level error amplification: single 1.0, centralized 4.4, hybrid 5.1, decentralized 7.8, independent 17.2.
limits: Computed from execution traces; the amplification term alone was not significant after controls (p=0.658).
agent_relevance: Supports guardrails that put a program-side check between every model output and the next step.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems (planning degradation)
finding: All multi-agent variants hurt sequential constraint satisfaction. Decentralized helps parallel web search a little.
numbers: PlanCraft: MAS variants -39% to -70% vs single agent. Dynamic web navigation: decentralized +9.2%. Tool-count x coordination beta=-0.096, p=0.002.
limits: One planning benchmark drives the -70% figure.
agent_relevance: Matches our split: the model fills slots, the code orders them. Parallelism only for independent sub-problems.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: First taxonomy of multi-agent LLM failures: 14 modes in 3 clusters (system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification).
numbers: 1642 annotated traces, 7 frameworks. Human agreement kappa=0.88 on 150 traces. LLM annotator agrees with humans: 94% accuracy, kappa=0.77. Failure rates 41% to 86.7% across frameworks.
limits: Open-source frameworks and GPT-4 / Claude 3 era models; annotations by LLM judge for most traces.
agent_relevance: Use the 14 modes as a checklist for our own loop failure logs.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST) (cluster shares)
finding: Failures split into design, misalignment and verification problems. Verification gaps are about a fifth of failures.
numbers: Cluster shares: system design 41.8%, inter-agent misalignment 36.9%, task verification 21.3%. Reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%; incomplete verification 8.2%; incorrect verification 9.1%; proceeding without asking for clarification 6.8%.
limits: Shares depend on which frameworks were sampled.
agent_relevance: Verification and clarification are the cheap places for code to add checks.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST) (interventions)
finding: Fixing roles and adding a verification step raised success without changing the model.
numbers: ChatDev with GPT-4o: better role specification +9.4% success; added high-level objective verification +15.6% on ProgramDev.
quote: many existing verifiers perform only superficial checks
limits: Single framework; authors say isolated fixes are not enough.
agent_relevance: Role clarity and an external objective check are measured, cheap wins.

source: Becker et al. (2025) Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity (METR)
finding: Randomised trial: experienced developers using AI tools were slower, while believing they were faster.
numbers: 16 developers, 246 tasks. Forecast 24% faster; post-hoc estimate 20% faster; measured 19% slower. Experts forecast 39% (economics) and 38% (ML) faster. Developers accepted fewer than 44% of generations.
limits: Small N of developers; mature repos they knew well; early-2025 tools; authors cannot rule out artifacts.
agent_relevance: People misjudge how well the joint system works. Measure joint outcomes, never trust self-report.

source: Becker et al. (2025) METR (time use)
finding: With AI, time shifted from coding and searching to prompting, waiting and reviewing AI output, plus more idle time.
numbers: Screen recordings covering 29% of hours; categories compared with and without AI.
limits: Descriptive, small sample.
agent_relevance: Review cost is real: a joint system moves work from producing to evaluating.

source: Shao et al. (2026) Collaborative Gym (ICLR 2026)
finding: Human-agent collaboration beats fully autonomous agents when real users judge, in a non-turn-taking setup.
numbers: Real condition win rates of best collaborative agent vs autonomous: 86% travel planning, 74% tabular analysis, 66% related work. 150 trajectories from real participants.
limits: Win rate judged by the same users who took part; three tasks.
agent_relevance: Support for a human checkpoint where preferences are latent.

source: Shao et al. (2026) Collaborative Gym (ICLR 2026) (simulated)
finding: With an LLM user simulator, collaborative agents deliver less often within a 30-step limit but better quality when they deliver.
numbers: Failures: agent ignoring human messages 46%, repeated messages 26%, repeating or omitting actions 33%.
limits: Simulated user is not a real person.
agent_relevance: Collaboration cost shows up as lost delivery; budget for it.

source: Shao et al. (2026) Collaborative Gym (ICLR 2026) (failure analysis)
finding: Communication and situational-awareness failures dominate in real use.
numbers: Communication failures 65% of cases, situational awareness 40% (real condition). Users spent 21-32% of actions on direct environment control.
limits: Annotation by the authors taxonomy.
agent_relevance: Common ground and state tracking are the weak spot, the exact thing JCS theory says a team needs.

source: Mozannar et al. (2025) Magentic-UI
finding: Light human feedback lifts an autonomous web agent substantially. Mechanisms: co-planning, co-tasking, action guards, memory.
numbers: Autonomous 30.3% task completion, with simulated user holding side information 51.9% (+71%). The agent asked for help in 10% of tasks. With a smarter simulated user 42.6%, help asked in 4.3% of tasks.
limits: Simulated users, not people; GPT-4o agent; below SOTA on GAIA.
agent_relevance: Asking only when stuck gives most of the gain at low cost: a model for our escalation rule.

source: Mozannar et al. (2025) Magentic-UI (usability)
finding: Real-user study found the interface usable, but not habit-forming.
numbers: SUS 74.58; 75% found it easy to use; only 41.7% would use it frequently.
limits: Small lab study.
agent_relevance: Oversight overhead limits adoption.

source: Bucinca, Malaya, Gajos (2021) To Trust or to Think
finding: Forcing a person to think before seeing the AI answer cuts overreliance. People dislike it.
numbers: N=199 analysed (260 recruited). When AI wrong, correct answers: simple explanation 0.03 vs forcing 0.09 overall; carb detection 0.08 vs 0.27. Simulated AI 75% accurate.
limits: Not an LLM; MTurk; nutrition task; forcing benefits high-Need-for-Cognition people more; overreliance not eliminated.
agent_relevance: A forcing step (commit first, then see the other answer) is a direct template for our schema.

source: Bansal et al. (2021) Does the Whole Exceed its Parts?
finding: Explanations did not create complementary team performance. They raised acceptance of the AI advice, right or wrong.
numbers: Three datasets, about 100 participants per condition, over 1500 participants across experiments.
quote: explanations increased the chance that humans will accept the AI's recommendation, regardless of its correctness
limits: Human and AI accuracy comparable; classic ML classifiers rather than LLMs.
agent_relevance: Fluent justification persuades. Do not let an agent explanation count as evidence.

source: Si et al. (2024) LLMs Help Humans Verify Truthfulness, Except When Convincingly Wrong
finding: ChatGPT explanations speed up human fact-checking but people follow them when wrong.
numbers: 80 crowdworkers. Hard claims: no aid 59%, retrieval 73%, explanation 74%. Time 1.01 vs 2.53 min per claim. When explanation wrong, accuracy 0.35 (+/-0.22) vs 0.56 (+/-0.24) with contrastive explanation (p=0.009).
limits: Small N; ChatGPT era; contrastive display cost some accuracy when the explanation was correct and did not beat search.
agent_relevance: Make the model argue both sides, then let code or a check settle it.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What LLMs Know and What People Think They Know
finding: Users overestimate LLM accuracy. Longer explanations raise confidence without raising accuracy. Matching wording to model confidence narrows the gap.
numbers: 301 participants across Experiments 1 and 2 (284 analysed). Example item: model confidence 0.46 vs human confidence 0.95.
limits: Multiple-choice and short answer questions only.
agent_relevance: Surface the model real uncertainty to the human side of the system.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) REL-A.I.: Interaction-Centered Measuring of Human-LM Reliance
finding: Reliance on an LLM depends on interaction context and tone, not language alone. Only the abstract was seen.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Abstract-level only.
agent_relevance: Reliance is a property of the pair, not of the model.

source: Simkute et al. (2024) Ironies of Generative AI
finding: Applies Bainbridge ironies of automation to GenAI. Four causes of lost productivity: role shift from producing to evaluating, workflow restructuring, interruptions, easy tasks easier and hard ones harder.
numbers: Review; no new experiment.
limits: Argument from literature, not measured here.
agent_relevance: Direct JCS-style framing for design: stable task allocation, continuous feedback.

source: Tomasev, Franklin, Osindero (2026) Intelligent AI Delegation
finding: Delegation framework covering authority, responsibility, accountability and trust. Warns of a zone of indifference where agents comply without scrutiny.
numbers: Conceptual; no benchmark.
limits: No measurements.
agent_relevance: Chains of agents let intent mismatch spread. Check at each hand-off.

source: Tomasev et al. (2026) Intelligent AI Delegation (ironies)
finding: Restates Bainbridge paradox: humans removed from routine work lose the situational awareness for edge cases. Argues agents should seek clarification on ambiguous directives.
numbers: Conceptual.
limits: Position paper.
agent_relevance: Supports bi-directional clarity as a design rule.

source: Sumers et al. (2024) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: Frames language agents by memory, internal and external actions, and a decision loop, drawn from production systems and cognitive architectures.
numbers: Survey framework; no benchmark numbers.
limits: Conceptual.
agent_relevance: Close to our program-decides, model-fills-slot split.

source: Vaccaro, Almaatouq, Malone (2024) When combinations of humans and AI are useful, Nature Human Behaviour
finding: Recalled, not opened (page redirected to login): on average human-AI combinations did worse than the best of human or AI alone; losses on decision tasks, gains on creation tasks.
numbers: From memory: 106 experiments, 370 effect sizes, mean Hedges g about -0.23. Not verified.
limits: Figures unverified this session.
agent_relevance: Key reference for where to place a human check; verify before use.

source: Dell Acqua et al. (2023) Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier
finding: Recalled, not opened: AI helps inside the capability frontier and hurts outside it.
numbers: From memory: 758 consultants; inside frontier about 12% more tasks, 25% faster, 40% higher quality; outside 19 percentage points less often correct. Unverified.
limits: Not verified this session.
agent_relevance: The joint system needs a way to detect the edge of competence.

source: Bainbridge (1983) Ironies of Automation; Klein et al. (2004) Ten Challenges for Making Automation a Team Player
finding: Recalled, not opened: automating the easy part leaves operators the hard part and skill decay; automation must be a team player with common ground.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not reopened.
agent_relevance: Source of design rules that Simkute and Tomasev revive.

source: Woods and Hollnagel (2006) Joint Cognitive Systems: Patterns in Cognitive Systems Engineering
finding: Unit of analysis is the person plus tools, defined by function, not by parts. Not opened; no free text found and the search budget was spent.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Book, not read.
agent_relevance: Supports measuring the whole loop and its control, not the model alone.
